Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
‐ Strategy: Staggered-adoption Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study (dynamic DID).  

‐ Justification  
  •  The “treatment” (adoption of a wrongful-discharge doctrine) occurs at clearly dated, state-specific court decisions that are plausibly orthogonal to contemporaneous establishment outcomes.  
  •  Adoption is staggered across states (and sometimes rescinded), giving both cross-section and time variation.  
  •  The data set is a long panel (1976-1999) that includes treated and never-treated states before and after each adoption, fitting the DID design.  
  •  Dynamic event-study coefficients allow (i) pre-trend tests, (ii) visualization of impact timing, and (iii) flexible treatment effects that may evolve with capital adjustment lags.  
  •  A modern implementation (Sun & Abraham 2021 or Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021) avoids the bias of two-way FE with heterogeneous treatment effects.  

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
  •  Dismissal protection indicator GFs,t = 1 if state s has the “Good-Faith” wrongful-discharge exception in force in year t; 0 otherwise.  
  •  We will also experiment with a three-level variable: 0 = no exception, 1 = public-policy or implied-contract only, 2 = good-faith.  

Control group  
  •  Establishments in states that have not yet adopted the exception by year t.  
  •  Never-adopters serve as long-run pure controls.  

Treatment timing / event date  
  •  Event year = first calendar year in which the state supreme court decision is in force (court date or first full fiscal year thereafter).  
  •  If a state subsequently overturns the doctrine, the treatment indicator switches back to 0 (allows difference-in-difference-in-reverse).  

No RDD is used, so no running variable / cutoff.  

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of adoption, treated and control states’ employment volatility, capital intensity, and TFP would have evolved in parallel.  
  •  Plausibility: Court cases are typically triggered by idiosyncratic wrongful-discharge disputes, not macro conditions. Many adoptions surprised the HR/labor-law community.  

A2. No anticipatory behavior: Firms could not perfectly foresee the exact year of adoption and change input decisions beforehand.  
  •  Plausibility: Although HR newsletters discussed the doctrines, litigation outcomes and timing were highly uncertain. We will still include leads in the event study to test.  

A3. Stable composition: The distribution of industries within state-year cells is not radically altered by treatment in ways that mechanically change outcomes (entry/exit balanced in aggregation).  
  •  Plausibility: LBD and ASM allow us to net out entry/exit directly; plus industry-year FEs mitigate mix changes.  

A4. No spillovers: Adoption in one state does not directly change establishments in another state (except via migration, which we will test).  
  •  Plausibility: Labor-law doctrines are state-specific; however, multi-state firms could reallocate activities. We test robustness by excluding multi-state firms using EIN identifiers.  

A5. Treatment exogeneity with respect to contemporaneous shocks: Other state policies do not systematically coincide with adoption.  
  •  Plausibility: We will control for time-varying state covariates (minimum wage, unemployment insurance tax base, union density, corporate tax rate, etc.).  

================================================================  
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Other synchronous policy changes (e.g., minimum-wage hikes, expansions of workers’ comp).  
  •  Mitigation: Add controls for those policies; include state×year covariates; show results are unchanged when dropping states that changed multiple labor laws in the same year.  

Threat 2: Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in two-way FE DID.  
  •  Mitigation: Use Sun & Abraham (2021) estimator (eventStudy function in fixest or did2s package) and Callaway-Sant’Anna group-time ATT.  

Threat 3: Migration / reallocation of establishments across state borders.  
  •  Mitigation: (i) Track plants by EIN; drop movers or assign them to state of origin; (ii) run specifications on immobile plants (single-state firms); (iii) placebo “destination-state” tests— examine whether plants moving into treated states drive results.  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
################## 0. Packages ##################
lib <- c("data.table","fixest","did","tidyverse")
install.packages(setdiff(lib, installed.packages()[,1]))
lapply(lib, library, character.only = TRUE)

################## 1. Load Data #################
# LBD state-industry-year file
lbd   <- fread("lbd_state_sic_year.csv")   # variables: state, sic2, year, emp, emp_change, entrants, exits
# ASM plant-year file
asm   <- fread("asm_panel.csv")            # variables: plant_id, state, year, k_stock, l_prod, l_nonprod, value_added, shipments, ...

# Policy file with adoption years
policy <- fread("wd_doctrines.csv")        # state, goodfaith_year, implied_year, publicpol_year, repeal_year

################## 2. Merge Policy ################
# Good-Faith dummy
policy[, treat_year := goodfaith_year]     # focus on good-faith
# Expand to panel
states <- unique(lbd$state)
years  <- 1976:1999
panel  <- CJ(state = states, year = years)
panel  <- merge(panel, policy, by = "state", all.x = TRUE)

panel[, gf := as.integer(!is.na(treat_year) & year >= treat_year & (is.na(repeal_year) | year < repeal_year))]

# Merge into LBD & ASM
lbd   <- merge(lbd, panel[,.(state,year,gf)], by=c("state","year"))
asm   <- merge(asm, panel[,.(state,year,gf)], by=c("state","year"))

################## 3. Construct Outcomes #########
# Example outcomes in ASM
asm[, capital_labor := k_stock / (l_prod + l_nonprod)]
asm[, log_lp := log(value_added/(l_prod + l_nonprod + 1))]
# TFP via Solow residual (simplified)
asm[, log_tfp := log(value_added) - 0.65*log(k_stock) - 0.35*log(l_prod + l_nonprod)]

################## 4. Main DID: Callaway-Sant’Anna #########
# Prepare data
asm_cs <- asm[!is.na(gf)]
asm_cs[, treat := ifelse(gf==1, year, 0)]   # event treatment year, 0 for never treated
cs_out <- att_gt(yname = "log_lp",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "plant_id",
                 gname = "treat",
                 xformla = ~ state + sic2,
                 data = asm_cs)

# Aggregate to overall ATT
agg_effect <- aggte(cs_out, type = "group")

summary(agg_effect)

################## 5. Event-Study with Sun & Abraham #########
asm[, rel_year := year - min(year[gf==1]), by = .(state)]
asm[, rel_year := fifelse(gf==0, NA_integer_, rel_year)]
# keep +/-6 years
asm_fe <- feols(log_lp ~ sunab(treat_year, year) |
                 plant_id + year + state#sic2,
                 data = asm)

iplot(asm_fe)   # pre-trend visual

################## 6. Robustness: Exclude multi-state firms ####
single_state_firms <- asm[, .(n_states = uniqueN(state)), by = plant_id][n_states==1]$plant_id
asm_ss <- asm[plant_id %in% single_state_firms]
feols(log_lp ~ sunab(treat_year, year) |
      plant_id + year + state#sic2,
      data = asm_ss)
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory (Lazear 1990; Bentolila & Bertola 1990) predicts that higher firing costs:  
  •  Reduce variance of employment adjustments (|ΔEmp|/Emp↓ by perhaps 10–15 %).  
  •  Increase capital-labor ratios (K/L↑) as firms substitute toward capital; magnitude ~5–10 %.  
  •  Shift skill mix toward non-production (higher retention of skilled workers).  
  •  Lower measured TFP if internal reallocation is hampered; plausible decline 2–3 %.  

Thus I expect negative effects on labor productivity and TFP and positive effects on capital deepening.  

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1. No pre-treatment trend differences .......... 0.8  
C2. No anticipation / timing manipulation ........ 0.7  
C3. No spillovers / SUTVA ........................ 0.6  
C4. Stable treatment assignment (no reversal) .... 0.9  
C5. No other simultaneous shocks ................. 0.6  

Average ≈ 0.72 → Reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.
